The X1 control board, explained

What the board does, how power and commands flow through it, how the control program thinks, and how to install it in the excavator. Pictures of the board are rendered from the real design files; the diagrams and the simulator follow the real firmware rules.

1 Big picture2 Board tour3 Power4 Driving a motor5 Try it6 Safety rules7 The program8 InstallationWords
Status: the board and its program are designed and every design check passes on the computer. Nothing has been built or run on real hardware yet. The hand controller (the "handle") is planned but not designed yet; until it exists, the motors can be tested from a computer over USB.

1The big picture

The board is the excavator's brain and its muscle switches. You move the sticks on a hand controller; it sends what you are doing by radio, 50 times a second. The board decides what each of the 7 motors should do, checks the safety rules, and sends battery power to the motors. It reports back 10 times a second (battery level, faults).

2A tour of the board

This is the real board as designed (96 × 64 mm, about the size of a playing card). Click a number, or press Play tour. Parts with a job together are grouped into one stop.

Top side. Outboard edge (towards the outside of the machine) at the top: USB-C and the radio antenna. Front edge on the right: the power socket. Inboard edge at the bottom: the motor connectors.

3Where the power goes

The battery gives 9 to 12.6 V. Every motor runs on it directly: the tracks, the swing and the arm's four actuators. Other parts need lower voltages, so the board makes two more: 5 V for lamps, buzzer and the future 4G module, and 3.3 V for the brain. Watch the moving dashes: they show which way the energy flows.

Why converters?

A converter is like a gearbox for electricity: it swaps voltage for current with little loss. Turning 12 V into 5 V this way wastes far less heat than simply "burning off" the extra volts.

Protected input

If the battery plug is ever wired backwards, a transistor at the input stays closed and nothing is harmed. A clamp swallows the voltage spikes that motors make.

Kind to the battery

The converter switches itself off below about 6.2 V, and the program stops the motors at 9.6 V, so a flat pack is not drained further. The fuse in the toolbox is 5 A; the worst case of every motor stalled at once is 4.45 A (5.04 A for the few seconds until the arm's own fuses and the stall rule act).

4How a motor driver works

Each motor has its own driver chip. Inside are four electronic switches arranged like the letter H around the motor (an "H-bridge"). Closing two opposite switches pushes current through the motor one way; the other pair pushes it the other way. The brain controls each driver with just two wires: direction and speed.

Speed is a fast on/off rhythm

The driver cannot give a motor "half a battery". Instead it switches power on and off very quickly and the motor feels the average. At 60 % it is on 60 % of the time. This is called PWM. On this board it happens 20 000 times a second; below it is slowed down a million times so you can see it.

It watches the current too

Each driver measures the motor's current and sends it to the brain on a third wire. If a motor is blocked, the driver itself limits the current: 1.03 A for the tracks, 0.6 A for the swing, 0.5 A for the arm. The program adds a second rule: a motor that draws about what it would draw if blocked for 2 seconds is switched off.

The "Brake" setting joins both motor wires together (switches C and D), which stops a motor quickly. "Asleep" opens every switch: the motor is free. While the machine is not armed, all seven drivers sleep.

What if…



Machine

Board

Radio link Machine E-STOP Battery Lights power   status Buzzerquiet Lamps 1   2 Packets

Dead band

A stick moved less than 12 % from centre counts as centred, so a thumb resting on it does nothing (the small dashed circle).

Smooth ramps

Speed never jumps: from stop to full takes 0.3 s for the tracks, 0.4 s for the swing (protects its gears) and 0.1 s for the arm.

The boom has two cylinders

Both get the same command. The board compares their currents and gently slows the stronger side (up to 15 %) so they stay level; a big difference for 3 s stops the boom. A re-sync button drives both fully in, to their end stops, to line them up again.

6The safety rules

The program never lets a motor run unless it is sure you are in control. After any stop, the machine is "disarmed" and only re-arms when the sticks are centred and no button is held, so nothing jumps when control comes back.

RuleWhat happensHow it clears
Radio lostNo valid command for 0.35 s: every motor stops at once, except the swing, which slows down over 0.4 s to protect its gears.The radio returns, then all inputs centred.
EMERGENCY STOPThe red button stops everything and the board remembers it ("latched"), even if the radio drops.Release E-STOP, centre the sticks, press RESUME.
Switching onThe motor drivers stay asleep until a valid command arrives with all inputs centred.—
Stalled motorA motor drawing 90 % of the current it would draw blocked at that speed (never more than its current limit) for 2 s is switched off (a blocked track, a rock against the swing, a jammed actuator).Let go: its input returns to centre.
Battery lowThe battery voltage is averaged over about 2 s, so a short dip does not trip it. Below 10.5 V: warning beeps. Below 9.6 V: motors stop.The averaged voltage is back above 10.5 V (charge the pack).
Boom out of stepThe two boom cylinders draw clearly different currents (over 130 mA apart) for 3 s, or one reaches its end and the other does not follow within 3 s: the boom stops. The other motors keep working.RESUME, or the re-sync button (drives both cylinders fully in to line them up).
Driver faultAny driver reporting overheating or a short stops everything.RESUME, once the fault is gone.

7Inside the control program

The program runs on the ESP32-S3 brain. It is written in two layers, so the important part can be tested on an ordinary computer:

The "hands": hardware layer x1_main.ino

Talks to the chip's pins: makes the 20 kHz speed signals, sets the direction pins, reads the current and battery sensors, runs the radio, lights the LED, sounds the buzzer, and offers a text console over USB.

The "head": decision layer control_logic.cpp

Every decision: which stick drives which motor, the ramps, the boom balancing and all the safety rules. It never touches a pin, so automatic tests on a PC check it (they all pass).

The rhythm: one slow-motion tenth of a second

The decision step runs every 2 ms (500 times a second). A command from the handle arrives every 20 ms. A status report goes back every 100 ms. Below, 0.1 s is stretched to 5 s.

Every decision step does four things, in this order (shown here much slower still):

1. Readmotor currents, battery voltage, driver fault line
2. Checkradio still alive? E-STOP? battery? stalls?
3. Decidemap sticks to motors, apply speed and ramps, balance the boom
4. Actset speed and direction of each driver, wake or sleep them, lamps, buzzer, LED

What a command contains

Both sticksposition of each axis, −1000…+1000
Buttonstrack ▲▼ ×2, E-STOP, RESUME, lamp 1, lamp 2, horn, boom re-sync
Speed setting20–100 % (steps of 5, starts at 65 %)
Check codecatches damaged packets

What the status report contains

Statearmed, radio link, E-STOP, pairing, re-sync
Faultsstall, battery, driver, boom
Measurementsbattery voltage, radio signal strength
Per motorspeed, current, flags

Pairing: only your handle is obeyed

8Installation, step by step

From a bare board to a working machine. Steps 1–2 happen at the desk, 3–5 when the body is assembled (see BODY.md, "Assembly order"), 6–8 at first switch-on.

1

Get the board made

Upload the files in controller/main_board/fab/ to JLCPCB: the Gerber zip (the board itself: 4 layers, 1.6 mm), the BOM (the parts list) and the CPL (where each part goes). They solder all 148 parts on the top side. Before ordering, check the part rotations in their placement preview; some parts in their library need a correction there.

2

Load the program, before it goes in the machine

A USB-C cable alone powers the brain (see section 3), so no battery is needed. In the Arduino IDE 2: install "esp32 by Espressif" version 3.x, open controller/firmware/x1_main/x1_main.ino, and choose:

BoardESP32S3 Dev Module
USB CDC On BootEnabled (the console needs it)
USB ModeHardware CDC and JTAG
Flash Size / Partition Scheme8MB / 8M with spiffs
PSRAMDisabled

Click Upload. Then open the Serial Monitor at 115200 and type show: the board answers with its state. The red light means power; the green light flashes briefly every 2 s while no handle is found.

If the computer does not see the board: hold BOOT, press and release RESET, release BOOT, then upload again.

3

Where it goes

The board sits in the side bay of the left body half (print B102), under the engine hood, on 4 posts moulded into the print. Parts face up, the USB-C and antenna edge faces the outside of the machine, the motor connectors face the middle. Fix it with 4 × M2.5 self-tapping screws, on the bench, before the half goes on the machine.

Left: inside the body with the printed shells hidden (3D model of the real board; parts shown as blocks). Right: close-up of the bay.

4

Plug in the motors and outputs

All plugs go into the row along the inboard edge. Each socket is labelled on the underside of the board, and every plug only fits one way round.

The underside: the labels under each socket. Cable routes (from BODY.md): the 4 track wires come up through the slip ring in the turntable's hub; the swing motor's wires come through the counterweight's channel and over the rear wall; both then run over the frame into the left bay.

5

Connect the power

The battery hangs under the hatch on top of the body (the raised engine hood, held by magnets); the switch, fuse and charging socket are in the toolbox on the right half. One XT30 cable (the "12 V link") runs from the toolbox to the board's yellow socket on its front edge. Leave about 150 mm of slack so a body half can be lifted off and set beside the machine before unplugging.

6

First switch-on and motor check

Stand the machine on a box so the tracks hang free, and make sure the arm can move freely. Plug in USB and open the Serial Monitor, switch on, then type:

zerocalibrates the 7 current sensors (nothing moves)
drive 1 30runs motor 1 at 30 % for 1 s. Motors: 1 left track, 2 right track, 3 swing, 4 or 5 boom (both sides together), 6 stick, 7 bucket
flip 3if a motor turned the wrong way, reverses that channel (remembered)
showstate, battery, currents and faults
helpthe full list

The bench drive refuses to run while a handle is linked, the E-STOP or a fault is latched, or the battery is low. The ramps and the stall, battery and fault rules still apply.

7

Pair the hand controller (once it exists)

Within 10 s of switching on, hold BOOT for 2 s (or type pair). The green light blinks fast for up to 60 s while the board waits for the handle (section 7). Do not hold BOOT while switching on or pressing RESET: that starts the chip's program loader instead.

8

Close up

With the body closed, the USB-C socket stays reachable through a slot in the left side, so you can update the program without opening anything.

Words used here

Actuator
A small motor that pushes a rod in and out (like a hydraulic cylinder). The arm has four: two for the boom, one for the stick, one for the bucket.
Boom, stick, bucket
The three parts of an excavator arm, from the machine outwards. Swing turns the whole upper body.
Armed / disarmed
Armed: the motors follow your commands. Disarmed: the drivers sleep and nothing moves.
Converter (buck)
A circuit that turns a higher voltage into a lower one efficiently (12 V into 5 V).
Regulator (LDO)
A simple circuit that makes a very clean, steady voltage (3.3 V for the brain).
ESP32-S3
The small computer on the board, with a built-in radio.
ESP-NOW
The direct radio link between the handle and the board, on 2.4 GHz like Wi-Fi but without a router.
H-bridge / motor driver
Four electronic switches around a motor that let it run either way. Each driver chip contains one.
PWM
Controlling speed by switching power on and off very fast; the share of "on" time sets the speed.
Current limit / stall
A motor that is blocked draws a lot of current; the driver caps it, and the program switches the motor off if it stays blocked.
Dead band
The small zone around a stick's centre that counts as "not touched".
Ramp
Changing speed gradually instead of in one jump.
Latched
Remembered until you clear it on purpose (E-STOP needs RESUME).
XT30, JST-XH, JST-PH
Plug types: XT30 (yellow) for battery power; XH and PH are small white plugs for motors, lamps and the expansion port.
Resettable fuse (PTC)
A fuse that cuts off on a short circuit and works again once the short is removed.
Gerber, BOM, CPL
The factory files: the board's layers, the parts list, and each part's position.
